newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Lukewarm response to strike call in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Lukewarm response to strike call in South Korea.

text.p: South Korean workers gave a half-hearted response on Wednesday to a strike call by an outlawed union group following President Kim Young-sam's stunning retreat over a controversial labour law.

Police picked up a fugitive leader from the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions but later released him in line with Kim's new spirit of compromise over the law, which he said on Tuesday could be sent back to parliament for debate.
Dan Byong-ho was one of seven confederation leaders holed up at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral. He was detained for two hours of questioning near the capital, a state prosecutor said.
Riot police have withdrawn from the church following Kim's order to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders.
But stocks fell sharply in early trading on fears Kim's reversal would delay restructuring of the economy, brokers said. The main index was down 2.02 percent at 676.59 points.
A Labour Ministry official said some workers in key industries such as automaking had downed tools.
"But we still don't know the full picture yet," he said.
The confederation said strikes once a week in protest at the law, which allows firms to sack workers and replace strikers, would go on until the government scrapped the legislation.
In a major concession to the opposition, President Kim, conceding that forced passage of the law had caused public anxiety and damaged the economy, agreed to send it back to parliament.
But Kim, who said the strife had defeated the law's aim of revitalising the economy, insisted dumping the legislation would go against the constitution and that it could only be revised.
He has said the law was needed to free up the labour market, thus trimming corporate costs and boosting competitiveness.
A Hyundai Motor Co Ltd union official in the southeast city of Ulsan said 29,000 confederation members joined the strike and that production would be halted for one day.
But Lee Chung-tak, a company public relations officer, said although production was slow, the factory was still running.
"About 30 percent of management, or white collar labourers, have joined the production lines," Lee told Reuters.
A union official from Ulsan-based Hyundai Heavy Industries, the nation's largest shipyard, said only 210 workers had joined the stoppages. Production would not be affected, he said.
Union members at automaker Kia Motors, located just outside Seoul, would hold partial strikes for four hours in the afternoon, a confederation union official said.
The confederation said it was expecting 182,000 workers in all sectors to heed the strike call on Wednesday.
At a meeting of the heads of three main political parties on Tuesday, Kim expressed sorrow for output losses of billions of dollars through strikes sparked by the law.
He also agreed to reopen debate on another controversial law reviving a once notorious domestic spy agency.
Both laws were rammed through parliament in a six-minute dawn session on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
According to an account of the meeting by opposition leader Kim Dae-jung of the National Congress for New Politics, Kim also indicated the confederation should be recognised.
Multiple trade union representation is a major demand of international labour organisations.
Kim's dramatic climbdown followed a decision by the confederation to call off indefinite stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week.
